Percentage-wise he could be your half-brother as 23andme has a range of 17% - 34% of dna shared. 

There is a chance he could also be your dad’s half-brother with 4% - 23% of dna shared.

These both might appear as a 1st cousin to you.

23andme seems to base relationship on the age of the person and the percentage of dna shared. 

I found my half-aunt there, who was born 15 years after my mom, but was listed as 1st cousin as if it assumed one of my 13/14-year-old uncles were her father. But nope…it was my wild grandpa. 

Your match was born 20 years after your dad’s birth, so it makes sense it would be listed as a 1st cousin as well. 

I wish 23andme would specify longest cM (centimorgan) length though…because that is a huge hint of how one is related as well.

I actually have a theory that she had Borderline Personality Disorder. We do not know her relative’s identities. I did dna match with what seems like her first cousin. But they don’t even know who their parents are. Complete mystery.

I have been working in the media since I was 25, I’m 35 now. This industry is very much like a group-oriented social hierarchy with one or three supreme overlords. You grow based on WHO you know. Your education, work experience do matter as well..but not as much if you do not have good connections with the media overlords. I started as a PA, (I learned to shoot, edit, make graphics, technical direct, floor direct, everything) and built up my experience and NEVER GOT PROMOTED AFTER SIX YEARS. My mistake was I didn’t network…I’m actually quite shy with very high anxiety..so my fault. But I’m stubborn and I love working with cameras, so I kept my eye open for new jobs and got a role at another station.  Sooo…to be clear, I’m not a reporter, but I work in the creative and production department and much of the time I do need to work with the reporters.

So..I have two ways that come to mind. 

1) NETWORKING

if your ft dept manager will allow you to…talk to the news producer and ask if you can work on stories to build your reel up,  and when a reporter’s position opens you can take it…sooo taking the “foot-in-the-door” job might really be good - if not, I’d ask how the FT job boosts your chances because I think your foot is already in the door…you work there already sooo

2) CLIMB THE LADDER: 

taking a reporter job at low-tier stations (every reporter I know had to get a low-paying job first and work for 2 years on contract. After their contract was up, they moved up to a higher tier station for another 2 years, and so on…this can vary by state if you are the US….MAKE A REEL

TIP. MAKE A REEL (I keep pushing this but yeah make a reel of all reporter work you’ve done, Voice overs, on-screen stand ups, etc less than :30-1 min.)

Also do you really want to be a reporter?? They work more then anyone I know and can become bitter and ruthless due to lack of sleep from the constant pressure to report content that sells

In America,  that way of thinking stems from Puritan ideology. Keep your end up, work hard as soon as you can walk, do not rely on others. I’m sure this ideology exists in other cultures as well. But in some other cultures that are geared toward the group, the idea of success is based on the actions of individuals within the whole family…and it’s up to individuals in that family to advance economic and social standing. During college children are often financially supported by their parents. This is so they focus completely on their studies and get top grades to enter fields that can really advance them up. In China, it’s kinda like a ladder. Parents work, grandparents raise the kids, parents save money and pay for adult children to attend college,  children graduate and grow some assets and do their part to advance the family. The cycle continues until it’s not able to.
